Course description

This course explores how to design and manage the physical, information, and financial flows that connect organizations across the supply chain. Using analytical frameworks, mathematical models, and real-world applications, you will learn to make strategic decisions related to supply chain network design, supply chain finance, supplier management and procurement, production and material requirements planning, distribution, Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP), and process and organizational design. By the end of the course you will be equipped to optimize supply chain networks, apply financial analysis to supply chain decisions, and lead cross-functional initiatives that balance operational excellence with strategic business objectives. This course is part of the MITx MicroMasters® Program in Supply Chain Management.

The widgets are transported by a dedicated carrier from the manufacturing sites through the DC to the regional warehouses.
In particular, the manufacturer has asked for your help in deciding how many DCs to use in the network, as well as which potential DC locations to use. Practice Problem 2: Papper
Papper is a paper goods manufacturer. One of their main paper products is a paper towel, which is produced in two (2) plants in the contiguous U.S. From the plants, the paper towels are sent to nine (9) regional warehouses (RW), from where they are then shipped to customers across the U.S.
The distribution manager at Papper wants to reduce the number of direct transports in the network, reduce the inventory levels at the plants, and move inventory closer to the regional warehouses, by introducing a central warehouse (CW) where all finished paper towels are stored before further shipment. That is, the idea is to have the towels flowing from the plants to the CW and then to the RWs. The CW will have a small safety stock, but everything that comes into the CW during a week should also leave the CW during that week.
The distribution manager has found five (5) candidate locations for the CW that he is now choosing between. Capacity is not an issue at any of them.

Practice Problem 4: Harley Stevenson

Once per week, finished bicycles are transported in large batches, using direct transports, from the manufacturing site to three (3) Distribution Centers (DCs). The DCs are all operated by third party providers, at the following weekly costs for HarleyStevenson:
DC1: Fixed cost: $2,000, Variable cost: $5 per bicycle
DC2: Fixed cost: $1,700, Variable cost: $6 per bicycle

Practice Problem 6: TIme-Expanded Network
In this problem, we will consider the following formulation of a time-expanded network problem.
Min \( z = \sum_{i} \sum_{j} \sum_{t} c_{ijt} x_{ijt} + \sum_{j} \sum_{t} h I_{jt} \)
s.t.
\( \sum_{j} x_{ijt} \leq S_{it} \quad \forall i \in S, t \in T \)
\( \sum_{i} x_{ijt} \geq D_{jt} \quad \forall j \in D, t \in T \)
\( \sum_{i} x_{ijt} - \sum_{i} x_{jit} + I_{j,t-1} - I_{jt} = 0 \quad \forall j \notin S, t \in T \)
\( I_{jt} = I_{jt}^{initial} \quad \forall j, t = 0 \)
\( x_{ijt} \geq 0 \quad \forall i,j,t \)
Part 1
0 points possible (ungraded)
In time-expanded models, we investigate the system across multiple time periods. This approach allows products within the model to move not just spatially but also temporally. Additionally, it permits products to move solely through time, enabling them to remain at the same network node across several periods.
Contrary to the standard transport or transshipment models, time-expanded models allow for explicit incorporation of inventory holding. In the formulation mentioned, \(h\) represents the inventory holding cost.

Practice Problem 7: Estimating Inventory
In supply chain network models, inventory costs are normally not considered for several reasons. It is still, however, possible to estimate the cost impact of inventory when designing the system.

The section operates more or less independently, and consists of two (2) plants, two (2) distribution centers (DCs), that support (4) retailers. All products that are produced in the plants are transported through the DCs to the retailers. Each DC handles only two retailers. The combined average demand at the four retailers is 20,000 units per week.
You want to create a network flow model to compare two possible network designs. In particular, you are interested in comparing the current design to one in which you have only one DC supporting all four retailers. Assume that demand is split equally between the two DCs.

retrieved.text: Week 1 · Overview of Supply Chain Design: Introduction to Supply Chain Design Welcome to CTL.SC2x, Supply Chain Design. Now it's preferred, but it's not required, that you've already taken SC1x, Supply Chain and Logistics Fundamentals. In that course, we covered a lot of the building blocks that we will utilize in this course. If you haven't, that's OK. We'll help you along, and I'll point you to references. So let's get started. We should all know by now what a supply chain is. And the definition that we like to use is that it's two or more parties, companies, organizations, some entity, linked by a flow of resources. Typically, this is material, physical material, information, and money, that ultimately fulfill a customer's request. So we think of it as managing flows. There's the information flow, and the primary information flow is the order. I place an order for something. Hopefully, it comes to me delivered. It's physical. And there's some kind of financial payment back. And there's also other information flows in between, usually the status of the delivery. So we really like to think about supply chains as you're managing these different types of flows. So we know what a supply chain is, and we know what they involve multiple parties, not just a customer and supplier, but usually that supplier's supplier, and their supplier, all the way down to the raw materials. This is a linear relationship, but that's not that common actually. Most supply chains are very complex with non-linear relationships. Something like this, very ugly, where I have my customers over here, my raw material, but they're different manufacturers of components. And I have many cases where my main customer is also one of my primary suppliers. So it's very complex and very nonlinear. And the nice thing about supply chains, what makes them so interesting is they take many different forms. So one classic form is that of a manufacturer. So let's say in this simple example, I'm a bicycle manufacturer. And I like to think of this as tier zero. So the things that I do or the starting point. I might have two suppliers, and I would call these tier one suppliers. They're my primary suppliers. They supply the hardware and the frame for my bicycles that I manufacture. They, in turn, have primary suppliers, but for me as a bike manufacturer, they're tier two.

Week 2, Lesson 2 · Video 1: Introduction OK. In this lesson, we're going to touch upon some more advanced topics in supply chain network design. Now we're not going to go into great depth here. What I want to do is give you a feel for some of these advanced concepts. So here's what we're going to talk about, these five topics. First, robustness, and by robustness, what we're trying to do is capture the effect that uncertainty has, and primarily, uncertainty in demand. So how do I handle this within the mixed integer linear program framework that we talked about? Then I'm going to talk about multi-commodity flow. So far, everything we've looked at is with a single commodity. That is, it doesn't matter where it's produced, or where it's demanded, the same unit is fungible. It can be used anywhere across that network. Now we're going to say they're different products, different SKUs, or different categories, and they all have to flow through the same system. So we'll see how we incorporate that. Then we'll move on to building and flexibility. This is somewhat related to robustness, but the idea here is, we want to set up the structure, our network, so that it makes it makes it easier to be more flexible, in case there's changes in demand. And we're going to look specifically at a concept called chaining. Then we're going to move into multi-time period models. These are, if I have to consider different periods of time, because so far we've assumed everything's one bucket of time, typically a year. Could be a month, could be a week. But we assume that it's a representative time period. In this case, with multiple time periods, we want to see what the effect is, for example, what happens in January influences what happens in February, influences what happens in March, and so on. This is more of a tactical planning model, and we'll see this again in other areas. But I wanted to introduce it here. And then finally, we'll talk about the thing that's been missing. The elephant in the room. The inventory considerations. Because if you've been paying attention, most supply chain network design approaches do not consider inventory in the network design. And so we'll talk about that one finally. OK. Let's get started.

Week 1 · Overview of Supply Chain Design: Roadmap of Supply Chain Design: SC2x To finish up this lesson, I want to give you a roadmap of SC2x, let you see what's coming down the pike, what you'll see for the rest of the course. So there's really four things we're doing here in SC2x. We're all talking about design, and we're going to start with the design of the physical flow, then the information flows, the financial flows, and then we'll talk about design of the supply chain organization and the metric system itself. So let me talk about each of these in turn. So for the physical flow, this is all about answering the question, how should my material flow through a supply chain? We'll approach purchase in three ways. We'll first start with modeling the problem. And you've seen these types of problems before if you've taken SC0x, which hopefully you have. We'll talk about transportation and transhipment problems, facility location problems. And then we'll combine them together in what's known as a supply chain network design problem. So we'll talk about how to formulate the problems, and then we'll talk about how to solve them. And all this solving is doing is finding a trade-off between the costs and the level of service, or different types of costs-- fixed and variable. Part 1: you believe cost is JUST proportional to widgets — no fixed piece, just cost = rate × widgets.
